title: 04. BM25 & Lexical Search: Bag-of-Words Assumption
summary: The bag-of-words (BoW) assumption treats a document as an unordered multiset of terms — word order and grammatical structure are discarded.

sections.title: ① Concept Explanation
sections.body: The bag-of-words (BoW) assumption treats a document as an unordered multiset of terms — word order and grammatical structure are discarded. This dramatically simplifies document representation: a document becomes a frequency map {term: count}. All classical retrieval models (Boolean, TF-IDF, BM25, query likelihood) rely on BoW. The assumption is computationally convenient but loses critical information: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" are identical under BoW. Modern neural models (BERT, dense retrievers) relax this by processing full token sequences.

sections.title: ④ Visual Explanation
sections.body:
```
BAG-OF-WORDS ASSUMPTION
══════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Sentence: "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"
  
  BoW Representation:
  {
    "the": 2, "quick": 1, "brown": 1, "fox": 1,
    "jumps": 1, "over": 1, "lazy": 1, "dog": 1
  }
  
  LOST: "the quick brown fox" vs "the brown quick fox" → IDENTICAL
  LOST: Position, syntax, grammar
  KEPT: Term identity, term frequency
  
  "dog bites man" BoW = "man bites dog" BoW
  {"dog":1, "bites":1, "man":1} = {"man":1, "bites":1, "dog":1}
  ─ Semantically OPPOSITE but BoW-IDENTICAL ─
```

quiz.question: What information is lost under BoW?
options: Apply Truncated SVD to the TF-IDF matrix to project into a lower-dimensional (100–300) dense latent space where synonymous terms are close.

quiz.explanation: (1) Word order and syntax — "not good" vs "good" are different in meaning but similar in BoW. (2) Sentence structure. (3) Coreference ("it", "they" lose their referents).

quiz.question: When does BoW work well despite its limitations?
options: Assign importance weights to terms and threshold functions replace binary match.
(1) Vocabulary mismatch (no synonym handling). (2) All common terms get low IDF — the model degrades on queries with only high-frequency terms.
IDF becomes negative — the term is so common it's anti-correlated with relevance.
When the presence/absence of key terms is the primary relevance signal.
quiz.explanation: When the presence/absence of key terms is the primary relevance signal. This is common in keyword search, document classification, and entity retrieval where term overlap strongly correlates with relevance.

quiz.question: What is the phrase query problem under BoW?
options: A document is "elite" for a term if the term is about the central topic of the document.
With |V|=1M dimensions and most entries being 0, vectors are extremely sparse.
|V| — the size of the vocabulary (number of unique terms).
New York" ≠ {"New", "York"} semantically. BoW matches documents with "New" and "York" anywhere, not necessarily adjacent.
quiz.explanation: New York" ≠ {"New", "York"} semantically. BoW matches documents with "New" and "York" anywhere, not necessarily adjacent. Positional indexes and phrase queries address this.

quiz.question: What is n-gram extension to BoW?
options: The query uses different words than the document. E.g., query = "heart attack", document = "myocardial infarction".
A retrieval model defines how to measure relevance between query and document.
An inverted index maps each unique term to a list (posting list) of document IDs where that term appears, with optional frequency and position data.
Include bigrams (n=2) and trigrams (n=3) as additional vocabulary items.
quiz.explanation: Include bigrams (n=2) and trigrams (n=3) as additional vocabulary items. "machine_learning" becomes a single token capturing the phrase. TF-IDF/BM25 can then weight it independently.
